notes.16:12: The verb vayyechele ("fell ill") appears with a Late Biblical Hebrew III-Aleph spelling rather than the usual III-He form, creating a sonic wordplay with rofe'im ("physicians") at the end of the verse.
notes.17:6: Literally "his heart grew high" (Qal of gbh). Elsewhere in Chronicles this idiom denotes pride (e.g., 26:16; 32:25), but with "in the ways of the LORD" it uniquely conveys bold devotion and courage.
notes.17:8: The qere (read form) is Shemiramoth; the ketiv (written consonants) reads wshmrymwt (Shemerimoth).
notes.17:13: The noun translated "supplies" (melakah) ordinarily means "work" or "business," but can also denote property or stores (cf. 1 Sam 15:9). Here the feminine noun takes the masculine verb form hayah.
notes.18:8: The qere (read form) is Micaiah (Mikayehu), matching 18:7; the ketiv (written consonants) displays the shorter spelling mykhw (Micahu).
notes.18:14: The Masoretic Hebrew reads the shortened form "Micah" (Mikah) here, rendered "Micaiah" for consistency with the rest of the chapter.
notes.18:29: Hebrew uses two infinitives absolute (Hithpael hithchappes and Qal bo) functioning as finite first-person verbs ("I will disguise myself and enter"), immediately contrasted with the explicit imperative addressed to Jehoshaphat.
notes.18:33: The qere (read form) is singular "your hand"; the ketiv (written consonants) is plural/dual "your hands."
notes.18:34: The Masoretic Hebrew uses the Hiphil participle maamid ("holding himself upright"), in contrast to the passive Hophal participle in 1 Kgs 22:35.
notes.19:2: Hebrew combines the interrogative particle with a modal infinitive construct (halarasha laazor), literally "Is it to help the wicked?", expressing moral rebuke.
notes.19:8: The Masoretic Text reads wayyashubu ("and they returned to Jerusalem," Qal of shub), referring to Jehoshaphat's company or the appointed judges; some ancient versions revocalize the text to read "for the inhabitants of Jerusalem."
notes.19:11: Hebrew hattob literally means "the good" (singular substantive), denoting the upright person who acts faithfully in judgment.
notes.20:1: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "some of the Ammonites" (meha-ammonim); the Septuagint reads "Meunites" (cf. 2 Chronicles 26:7), which many textual critics regard as a letter transposition.
notes.20:2: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "from Aram"; many commentators conjecture an original reading "from Edom" given the similarity of the Hebrew letters dalet and resh and the southern location of En-gedi.
notes.20:20: The Hebrew plays on two stems of the same root (aman): the Hiphil imperative "trust" (ha'aminu) and the Niphal imperfect "you will be made secure" (te'amenu).
notes.20:25: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "corpses" (u-fegarim); some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions reflect "garments" (u-vegadim).
notes.20:35: The verb "allied himself" (etchabbar) is an Aramaized Hithpael perfect using an initial aleph prefix instead of the standard Hebrew he.
notes.21:2: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "king of Israel," a title the Chronicler occasionally applies to kings of Judah (cf. 21:4; 28:19). The first and fourth sons are spelled Azariah (Azaryah) and Azariahu (Azaryahu), variant forms of the same name.
notes.21:17: Jehoahaz (Yeho'achaz) is an alternate form of the name Ahaziah (Achazyahu, 22:1), reversing the position of the divine name element.
notes.21:19: Literally "to days from days, and at the time of the going out of the end to two days," an idiomatic construction in which "days" (yamim) denotes years.
notes.21:20: Literally "without desire" (be-lo chemdah), an idiom meaning no one lamented or regretted his death.
notes.22:2: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "forty-two years old"; the parallel in 2 Kings 8:26 and several ancient versions read "twenty-two."
notes.22:6: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "Azariah" (Azaryahu), a variant or scribal interchange for Ahaziah (Achazyahu; cf. 22:1, 7; 2 Kings 8:29).
notes.22:7: "Downfall" translates a rare Hebrew noun (tevusah, occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible) derived from a root meaning "to trample down."
notes.22:10: The Masoretic Hebrew reads vattedabber (Piel of d-b-r), understood here either from a rare root meaning "to destroy" or as an early scribal variant of vatte'abbed ("she destroyed," Piel of a-b-d) in 2 Kings 11:1.
notes.23:9: Hebrew pairs maginnot ('shields') with shelatim ('bucklers'), a rarer term whose exact sense is debated between a type of small or ceremonial shield and a quiver.
notes.23:13: The phrase 'directing the praise' translates modi'im lehallel, a Hiphil participle of yada with a Piel infinitive construct of halal, literally 'making known to praise,' meaning leading or cueing the musical praise.
notes.23:15: The idiom 'they laid hands on her' translates wayyasimu lah yadayim (literally 'they placed hands for her'), which is understood either as seizing her or as making room for her to pass.
notes.23:18: The Masoretic Hebrew reads hakkohanim halwiyyim ('the Levitical priests') without a conjunction between the two nouns.
notes.24:7: The phrase 'that wicked woman' translates hammirsha'at, a unique abstract feminine noun literally meaning 'wickedness,' used concretely to characterize Athaliah.
notes.24:13: The clause 'restoration progressed' renders watta'al arukha, an idiom literally meaning 'healing went up' (like new flesh closing a wound), applied to repair work.
notes.24:14: The expression 'for offering up' translates the Masoretic Hiphil infinitive construct weha'alot (from alah), coordinated with sharet ('ministering') to designate utensils used in offering sacrifices.
notes.24:25: The Masoretic Hebrew reads plural bene ('sons') in 'the blood of the sons of Jehoiada,' though only Zechariah is named in verses 20-22; some ancient versions harmonize to the singular.
notes.24:27: Ketiv/Qere: the ketiv (written text) reads w-r-b ('and the multitude/greatness of'), whereas the qere (read text) translated here reads yireb, an apocopated Qal imperfect of rabah ('increased' or 'grew great'). The noun massa can mean either 'oracle' or 'burden.'
notes.25:8: The Masoretic Text lacks a negative particle before the Hiphil imperfect yakhshilkha ("will cause you to stumble"); the Qal imperatives ("go, act, be strong") are thus read concessively or ironically as a warning that Amaziah will still face defeat if Israel marches with him.
notes.25:16: The verse plays threefold on the root ya'ats ("counsel"): the Qal participle yo'ets ("counselor"), the Qal perfect ya'ats ("has determined"), and the noun atsati ("my counsel"), continuing in v. 17 with the Niphal vayyivva'ats ("took counsel").
notes.25:23: The Masoretic Text calls Amaziah's grandfather Jehoahaz (an alternate name for Ahaziah, as in 21:17 and 22:1) and names the second gate sha'ar ha-poneh (Qal participle of panah, literally "the Turning Gate"), corresponding to "the Corner Gate" (sha'ar ha-pinnah) in 26:9 and 2 Kings 14:13.
notes.25:24: The Masoretic Text omits an explicit finite verb ("he took") before the direct-object phrases marked by et, leaving it to be supplied from context (compare 2 Kings 14:14).
notes.25:28: The Masoretic Text reads "in the city of Judah" (be'ir Yehudah), whereas the parallel in 2 Kings 14:20 reads "in the city of David."
notes.26:3: Follows the Qere Yekolyah ("Jecoliah"); the Ketiv is spelled Yekilyah.
notes.26:5: Literally "in the seeing/visions of God" (bi-r'ot ha-elohim, Qal infinitive construct of ra'ah, "see"); the Hiphil participle ha-mevin ("having understanding") with the preposition be- parallels Daniel 1:17.
notes.26:7: Follows the Qere ha-arvim ("the Arabs"); the Ketiv writes the longer gentilic plural form ha-arviyim.
notes.26:11: Follows the Qere Ye'i'el ("Jeiel"); the Ketiv reads Ye'u'el ("Jeuel").
notes.26:21: Follows the Qere ha-chofshit ("a separate house," literally "house of separation/isolation"); the Ketiv reads the abstract feminine noun ha-chofshut.
notes.27:5: A kor is a dry measure equal to ten ephahs (roughly 220 liters or 6 bushels); the Hiphil heshivu ("rendered," literally "returned") is an idiom for paying recurring tribute.
notes.27:6: The Hithpael vayyitchazzeq ("grew strong") echoes the recurring chazaq ("strong") motif across chapters 25-27, while the Hiphil hekhin ("established," literally "made firm/prepared") denotes steadfastly directing his conduct before God.
notes.28:3: The Hebrew text reads wayyab'er (Hiphil of ba'ar, 'burned'), stating directly that Ahaz burned his sons in the fire, rather than the idiom 'made pass through the fire' found in 2 Kings 16:3.
notes.28:16: The Masoretic Hebrew reads the plural 'kings of Assyria' (malke Ashshur), even though verse 20 names the single king Tilgath-pilneser; the plural is retained here without harmonizing to the ancient versions.
notes.28:19: The Hebrew calls Ahaz 'king of Israel' (and refers to 'the kings of Israel' in 28:27), reflecting Chronicles' regular practice of applying the covenant name 'Israel' to the Davidic kingdom of Judah.
notes.28:20: Tilgath-pilneser preserves the Chronicles spelling (Tillegath-pilne'eser) of Tiglath-pileser. The verb chazaqo (Qal of chazaq with an object suffix) functions transitively here in the sense 'strengthened him,' contrasting with 'brought distress upon him.'
notes.29:8: Ketiv reads lezeva'ah while Qere reads leza'avah, metathesized forms of the same noun meaning 'an object of trembling or terror'; the translation follows the Qere.
notes.29:13: Ketiv reads Jeuel (Ye'u'el) while Qere reads Jeiel (Ye'i'el); the translation follows the Qere. The same Ketiv/Qere vowel shift appears in 29:14 (Ketiv Jehuel, Qere Jehiel), where the Qere is likewise followed.
notes.29:24: The verb waychatte'u is the Piel denominative of chata' ('offer as a sin offering / purify from sin'), taking 'their blood' as direct object with directional 'against/on the altar.'
notes.29:28: Ketiv reads mechatzetzerim (reduplicated participle) while Qere reads machtzerim (Hiphil participle of chatzar, 'sounding trumpets'); the translation follows the Qere. Both 'the song singing' and 'the trumpets sounding' use collective metonymy for the choir and trumpeters.
notes.29:36: Hebrew prefixes the definite article directly to a finite Hiphil perfect verb in hahekhin ('that which [God] had prepared'), a distinctive Late Biblical Hebrew relative construction common in Chronicles.
notes.30:3: The compound adverbial form lemadday (literally 'for what is enough') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes 'sufficiently' or 'in sufficient numbers.'
notes.30:18: The Masoretic verse division separates the preposition be'ad ('for') at the end of verse 18 from its object ('everyone who sets his heart...') at the start of verse 19. The Piel verb yekhapper with be'ad literally means 'make atonement for' and carries the sense of granting pardon.
notes.30:21: The phrase 'instruments of might' (kele-'oz) is a literal rendering of the Hebrew expression denoting loud or resounding musical instruments used in temple praise.
notes.30:22: The Masoretic text reads wayyo'khelu ('and they ate') with hammo'ed ('the appointed feast'), referring metonymically to eating the sacrificial festival meals over the seven days. The Hithpael participle mitwaddim ('making confession') differs in stem from the Hiphil 'giving thanks' in 31:2, though in this context it may encompass both confession and grateful acknowledgment.
notes.31:7: The clause literally reads 'they began the heaps to lay a foundation' (leyissod, an unusual infinitive construct form of the verb yasad, 'to found/lay a base'), meaning they began piling up the base of the heaps of tithes.
notes.31:10: Three consecutive infinitives absolute ('akhol wesavoa' wehoter, 'eating and being satisfied and leaving over') function as finite verbs, a characteristic feature of Late Biblical Hebrew. The particle 'et before 'this great store' marks an emphasized nominative rather than a direct object.
notes.31:12: Here and in 31:13 the Ketiv writes the name with a waw (kwnnyhw), while the Qere omits the waw (konanyahu, vocalized with qamets qatan), rendered 'Conaniah.'
notes.31:17: Verses 16-18 use the Hithpael infinitive construct hityaches ('genealogical enrollment') nominally, introduced in verse 17 by the topicalizing particle 'et and continued in verse 18 by ulehityaches ('including enrollment').
notes.32:5: The Hebrew clause literally reads "and he raised up upon/to the towers," using an apocopated wayyiqtol of alah (interpreted as Hiphil with the wall as implied object) and Late Biblical Hebrew al in the sense of "up to."
notes.32:15: The Hiphil verb translated "will rescue" (yatsilu) is masculine plural with "your God" (eloheikhem), contrasting with the singular verb in v. 14 and reflecting the plural form of elohim or the Assyrian speaker's polytheistic perspective.
notes.32:21: Translated from the qere (umiytsiei meav), combining partitive min with the plural construct of the adjective yatsi ("those who come forth") before "his inward parts/body," meaning some of his own offspring; the ketiv writes a variant ending with waw.
notes.32:22: The Masoretic Text reads a Piel wayyiqtol of nahal ("guided/cared for them on every side"), whereas the Septuagint and Vulgate reflect a different Hebrew reading meaning "gave them rest on every side" (from Hiphil nuach).
notes.32:28: The Masoretic Text literally reads "and flocks for the folds" (using a metathesized spelling, averot, beside uravot "stalls" earlier in the verse), rather than reversing the terms to "folds for the flocks."
notes.33:7: The Masoretic Text preserves the unique spelling le-eilom, an Aramaizing or variant form of le-olam ("forever").
notes.33:13: "He accepted his plea" translates the Niphal wayyiqtol of atar (meaning to let oneself be favorably moved by a plea); the same verb recurs as a Niphal infinitive construct in v. 19.
notes.33:16: Translated from the qere vayyiven (Qal wayyiqtol of banah, "built/rebuilt"); the ketiv reads vayyakhen (Hiphil wayyiqtol of kun, "restored/established").
notes.33:19: The Masoretic Text vocalizes Chozai as a proper name ("Hozai"), whereas the Septuagint and some interpreters take the word as "the seers" or "his seers" (compare v. 18).
notes.34:4: The Hebrew term chammanim refers to incense altars or stands, here positioned atop the altars of the Baals. The closing phrase renders an elliptical Hebrew construction, literally 'the graves, those sacrificing to them.'
notes.34:6: The Qere reads a single word whose consonants are widely understood as 'in their ruins' (from chorbah), although the Masoretic patach vocalization formally matches 'with their axes' or 'swords' (from cherev, cf. Ezek 26:9). The Ketiv splits the letters into two words of uncertain sense.
notes.34:9: The Qere reads 'and they returned to Jerusalem' (Qal of shuv), referring to returning after gathering the funds, whereas the Ketiv reads 'and the inhabitants of Jerusalem' as an additional source of the collection.
notes.34:22: The phrase 'and those whom the king had sent' renders an elliptical Hebrew expression, literally 'and whom the king.' Also, the Qere spells Tokhath defectively while the Ketiv writes it plene with a waw.
notes.34:25: The Qere vocalizes 'burned incense' in the Piel stem, the standard stem in Chronicles for illicit offerings, while the Ketiv consonants indicate the Hiphil stem.
notes.35:3: The Qere reads 'who instructed' (Hiphil active participle of bin), while the Ketiv writes a form with waw suggesting either a passive sense ('who were instructed') or an orthographic variant.
notes.35:4: The Qere reads a Hiphil imperative ('make preparations' or 'prepare yourselves'), whereas the Ketiv reads a reflexive Niphal imperative ('be ready' or 'prepare yourselves').
notes.35:5: This concise verse pairs two rare Hebrew nouns for family subdivisions (peluggoth and chaluqqah) to match each lay family grouping with a corresponding Levitical family division.
notes.35:13: The Hebrew uses the same Piel verb (bishshel, 'cook') in both clauses, combining the fire of Exodus 12:9 with the verb of Deuteronomy 16:7 for the Passover while specifying pots, kettles, and pans for the other holy offerings.
notes.35:21: Literally 'the house of my war,' meaning the dynasty or kingdom with which Neco was fighting; the Piel infinitive of bahal ('to hurry me') conveys divine urgency.
notes.36:7: Or 'his temple'; the Hebrew noun hekal can denote either a royal palace or a temple.
notes.36:9: The Masoretic Text reads 'eight years old'; the parallel account in 2 Kings 24:8 and some ancient versions read 'eighteen years old.'
notes.36:10: Hebrew literally reads 'his brother,' using the noun broadly for a close male kinsman; according to 2 Kings 24:17, Zedekiah was Jehoiachin's uncle.
notes.36:15: 'Rising early and sending' translates paired Hebrew infinitives absolute (Hiphil of shakam and Qal of shalach), an idiom expressing earnest, persistent action.
notes.36:21: Or 'enjoyed'; the Hebrew verb ratsah here can mean either 'to pay off, make good' or 'to take pleasure in, enjoy,' echoing Leviticus 26:34, 43.

unplaced.text: He was twenty-five years old when he began his reign, and he reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem.
